title: Using Malware Detection Techniques for HPC Application Classification
problem: HPC systems lack reliable methods to classify application executables and identify unauthorized or malicious software. Existing job-name or resource-usage-based classification approaches are unreliable and fail to capture behavioral variations caused by different inputs or system noise.
motivation: Preventing computational resource waste, misuse, and unauthorized software execution while maintaining security and compliance in HPC environments.
method: The approach uses similarity-preserving fuzzy hashes (SSDeep) to generate fingerprints of HPC application executables. A Random Forest Classifier compares the similarity of these fuzzy hashes to classify applications and identify unknown samples. The method is evaluated on a dataset containing 92 application classes and 5333 distinct application samples.
key_novelty: Applying malware detection techniques based on fuzzy hashing to classify and identify HPC applications, including previously unseen samples.
contributions: A fuzzy hash-based classification method using SSDeep hashes with Random Forest for reliable HPC application identification
Demonstration that similarity-preserving fuzzy hashes can accurately classify unknown application samples on HPC systems
Evaluation on substantial dataset achieving 90% macro f1-score across 92 application classes with 5333 samples
Addresses critical security and compliance needs by enabling effective application classification to minimize resource waste and prevent unauthorized software

metrics.accuracy: macro f1: 90%, micro f1: 89%, weighted f1: 90%

limitations: Limitations and comparisons against alternative classification approaches are not discussed in the abstract.
